## pencil
The Pencil MCP server is the editor for .pen design files (web/mobile apps and websites). Use it to read, generate, and validate designs.

.pen files are encrypted: access them only via "pencil" MCP tools — never use Read or Grep on .pen files. Follow each tool's input schema exactly.

Always call get_editor_state(include_schema: true) if you don't have the current .pen file schema in the context. Knowing the schema is required to use any other Pencil MCP tool.

Tools: get_editor_state, get_guidelines, batch_get, batch_design, snapshot_layout, get_screenshot, get_variables, export_nodes, export_html.

- code-review: Review the changes since a fixed point (commit, branch, tag, or merge-base) along two axes — Standards (does the code follow this repo's documented coding standards?) and Spec (does the code match what the originating issue/PRD asked for?). Runs both reviews in parallel sub-agents and reports them side by side. Use when the user wants to review a branch, a PR, work-in-progress changes, or asks to "review since X".
- domain-modeling: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when the user wants to pin down domain terminology or a ubiquitous language, record an architectural decision, or when another skill needs to maintain the domain model.
- grilling: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan, decision, or idea. Use when the user wants to stress-test their thinking, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.
- prototype: Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question. Use when the user wants to sanity-check whether a state model or logic feels right, or explore what a UI should look like.
- resolving-merge-conflicts: Use when you need to resolve an in-progress git merge/rebase conflict.
- tdd: Test-driven development. Use when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions "red-green-refactor", or wants integration tests.
- releases: CipherBox v2 release and staging-deploy mechanics — release-please layout, the two version surfaces, staging tag pipeline, and the v1 freeze. Use when cutting a release, deploying to staging, or touching release/versioning config.
- crypto-privacy-review: Review code for cryptographic security, generate test cases and edge cases
- resolve-pr-reviews: Resolve PR Review Comments
- ship: Ship
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

11	**Wave 6 is DONE.** Merged 2026-08-07 in order: #1118 (`77ad6a71e`) → #1116 (`879090c1d`) → #1120 (`d2a75db8f`) → #1123 (`2ec86e565`) → #1119 (`868f1e656`) → #1122 (`99a88ed1b`) → #1117 (`2819cb831`). #1115 CLOSED unmerged, its three items folded into umbrella #872 (branch preserved). See [[project-wave4-review-queue-state]] for the review-cycle mechanics, which held.
12	
13	## The wave's defect class: trust an unsigned field
14	
15	Three independent PRs turned out to have the same shape — **a field outside the owner's signature trusted to identify something**: #1116 (`directChildScopeIndex`), #1120 (per-structure signer), #1119 (`recipientIdentityPk`). The fix each time was to re-derive the identifier from committed material rather than read it.
16	
17	**#1127 is the same pattern, unfixed** — `reseal_scope_root` (`crates/engine/src/rotation/reseal.rs:277`) seals to `recipientEncPk` with no tag re-derivation, so a write-grantee that swaps it redirects every future honest re-seal, the owner's included. Natural wave-7 opener. See [[feedback-security-gate-audit-binding-surface-upfront]].
18	
19	## Rebasing a queue: what actually caught things
20	
21	- **The predicted conflict was not the real one.** I forecast a `blueprint/engine.md` conflict between #1123 and #1120; it never happened (different sections). The break that *did* happen was #1123 vs already-merged #1118 — both `mergeable=CLEAN`, caught only by running the full workspace suite on the rebased tree. Reinforces [[project-semantic-merge-conflict-shape-change]].
22	- **Recipe per rebase:** diff the two file-name sets (`comm -12`) to size the risk, then run the suite that spans them. Disjoint file sets across languages (Rust-only PR vs `apps/web`-only PR) genuinely need no cross-check.
23	- **Rebuild `packages/client` dist before any `apps/web` typecheck** when main moved `worker/*` — see [[project-cross-package-dist-staleness]].
24	- **`BEHIND` vs `CLEAN`:** a PR one commit back that reports `mergeStateStatus=CLEAN` needs no rebase — the ruleset does not require up-to-date branches. Don't rebase reflexively.
25	- Run every gate **unpiped** and read `$?`. Piping a gate through `tail` gave a false 0 and pushed a `TS2339` break to CI on #1117.
26	
27	## Do not claim a PR merged without reading state
28	
29	I listed #1119 as merged in a summary when it was still `OPEN`; the user caught it. Merge status comes from `gh pr view --json state` or a `(#NNNN)` hit in `git log origin/main`, never from the flow of the conversation.
30	
31	## CodeRabbit slot economics
32	
33	Slots are 1/hr and **do not accumulate** — an unused hour is lost, not banked. Flipping a draft to ready spends the slot whether or not you wait for the verdict, so "merge without re-review" saves wall-clock, not slots. Weigh a re-review against CR's *demonstrated* yield on that PR: on #1123 it was two Minor maintainability notes and zero correctness catches, and it structurally cannot see cross-PR interaction. Land a known fix *before* the slot opens so the review covers it.
34

When batching v2 issues into parallel PRs, the binding constraint is hot-file contention, not the
number of actionable issues. Re-confirmed 2026-08-04 against main `3c08517d3` after six merges.

Standing hot files:

- `crates/engine/src/facade.rs` (5300+) and `crates/engine/tests/write_plane.rs` (4800+) — touched
  by almost every engine issue
- `crates/engine/src/sync/drain.rs` — settings, op-queue, pin-provider, device-state clusters
- `crates/engine/src/gate/floor.rs` + `seams/floor_store.rs`
- `crates/wasm/src/seams_bridge.rs` — NOT `host.rs`; seam-shape changes land next door to host.rs
- `apps/web/src/engine/snapshotStore.ts`, `packages/client/src/leaderRelay.ts`

The #635 rotation cluster is its own contention zone — `rotation/trigger.rs` (279 lines, 3
contenders), `net/rotation.rs`, `rotation/rotate_write.rs`, `rotation/sweep.rs`,
`rotation/reseal.rs` + `rotate.rs`.

**Why:** facade.rs is 5000+ lines so different functions usually auto-merge, but signature/shape
changes ripple. The recurring failure is the semantic merge conflict in
[[project-semantic-merge-conflict-shape-change]] — two PRs both MERGEABLE that break main's compile
pairwise.

**How to apply:** batch so each PR *owns* its hot files exclusively, and sequence any PR carrying a
signature change ahead of everything touching its callers. Group small issues that collide on the
same interface into ONE PR rather than trying to parallelize them — this also conserves the
CodeRabbit quota (see [[feedback-keep-prs-draft-control-cr-timing.md]]). Reserve worktree isolation
for the batches that genuinely run concurrently.

**Re-confirm the map after every merge wave.** Closing issues retires rows, but merges also *create*
rows — and a file's contenders are not always the ones named in the issue bodies (e.g. #793 reads as
a `gate/adoption.rs` issue but also edits `rotation/reseal.rs`, colliding with a different wave).
Repo-wide sweeps like a comment-hygiene pass collide with everything; run them alone.

---
name: project-gh-rest-parent-field-false-negative
description: "gh api /issues/N --jq '.parent' ALWAYS returns null — the REST payload has no parent object; every orphan check built on it is a false negative"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 8ed080ed-fffa-498c-9012-8e777bd9ef50
  modified: 2026-08-05T22:52:54.789Z
---

`env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh api /repos/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/<N> --jq '.parent.number'` **always
returns `null`**, whether or not the issue has a parent. The REST issue payload carries no `parent`
object — the field is **`parent_issue_url`**.

So any "find the orphans" sweep written against `.parent` reports **every** issue as an orphan.
Verify parentage only via `.parent_issue_url`, or authoritatively via
`GET /repos/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/<parent>/sub_issues`. GraphQL's `parent` field does work, but
GraphQL times out on this repo often enough that REST is the usual path.

**Companion trap, same pass (2026-08-06): a track umbrella reading "0 open children" can be an
artifact of missing parentage, not completeness.** #989 (core) showed 12/12 closed and looked
ready to close — but #1050, live core-track work, was orphaned and therefore invisible in the
rollup. After parenting it read 12/13 with one open child. **Always parent the orphans BEFORE
evaluating any umbrella for closure**, never after. #990 (api) survived the same check and is
genuinely 8/8 — but note that "no open children" only proves no *tracked* work remains.

Related: [[feedback-use-github-native-issue-dependencies]] (the dependency API is keyed by the
database `id`, not the issue number — the same shape of trap one level over).

You are doing GitHub issue-tracker hygiene on repo `FSM1/cipher-box` (a local checkout is at /Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box, branch main, clean).

## Hard constraints (read these first)

- ALWAYS run the gh CLI as `env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh ...`. Without the `env -u` prefix auth fails.
- An issue's parent is the REST field **`parent_issue_url`**. The field `.parent` is ALWAYS null in the REST payload — never use it, it produces false "orphan" results.
- The GitHub sub-issue API is keyed by the **database `id`**, not the issue number:

engine: implement the concrete WriteWavePublisher over the real seams
open
## Why this is not wiring

`WriteWavePublisher` (`crates/engine/src/rotation/rotate_write.rs`) is the write-plane rotation's transport edge. #1014 landed the two read-plane seams over the real network plane and deliberately stopped short of this one: three of its five methods are plumbing, but `republish` cannot be implemented against the seam as it stands.

Both blocking questions are now answered by **[ADR 0004 — Read-body child names are rewritten by the write-plane name wave](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/blob/main/decisions/0004-read-body-child-names-on-the-name-wave.md)** (FSM1/cipher-box-next#58, merged). **Read it before starting** — it settles a second, larger gap that this issue originally did not name.

## What the ADR settles

**D1 — the publisher re-resolves; it is not handed the authoring material.** The record handed to `republish` carries only routing identity:

```rust
pub struct RepublishedNode {
    pub node_id: [u8; 16],
    pub new_name: IpnsName,
    pub write_epoch: u64,
    pub is_root: bool,
}
```

Authoring at `new_name` additionally needs the node's read body, the read key it seals under, and the predecessor name. Widening this struct does not work as stated, because the orchestrator does not hold that material either — `WriteScopeNode` is `{node_id, current_name, child_node_ids}` — so it would mean widening `WriteSubtreeResolver` too, and dragging O(subtree) bodies and per-node key material through a primitive that currently holds exactly one secret.

Instead: add **`current_name: IpnsName`** to `RepublishedNode`, and let the concrete publisher do the gated read at `current_name` and author at `new_name`. This mirrors the landed read-plane precedent — `OwnerRotationNet::publish_scope_root` already does exactly this, and says so in code: *"The read body and the envelope fields a republish preserves come from the node's own current record, gated — the rotation carries neither."* The resume contract stays trivially intact: `is_republished(new_name)` is unchanged and still answers from published state alone.

**D2 — the read body cannot be carried verbatim.** `ChildRef.ipns_name` (`crates/core/src/seal/body.rs`) lives in the **read** body. The wave moves every node in the subtree to a freshly derived name, so afterwards every parent's child refs name nodes that have moved, and once interior old names batch-retire they name nothing.

Write-grantees are fine — they derive names from `writeScopeSeed`. **Read-only survivors cannot**: `open_grant_blob` returns `write_scope_seed: None` for a read-only grant, and the re-point object carries `currentRootName` and no other name. So without a rewrite, a read-only grantee reaches the new root and cannot descend. #26 D3's "read-only survivors follow republished mirrors" was pointing at exactly this and was never elaborated; the blueprint dropped the clause entirely.

So the wave **rewrites each `ChildRef.ipnsName`** to the child's freshly derived name and re-seals the read body under the node's unchanged read key at the unchanged read epoch. Child-first ordering already makes every child's new name known before its parent publishes.

## Scope

1. **Widen `RepublishedNode` with `current_name`** and update `rotate_scope_write`'s call site plus the simulation tests.
2. **Land the concrete `WriteWavePublisher`** over `RecordTransport` + `ApiClient`:
   - `register` / `retire` over `net::register` and `net::retire` — already bounded and idempotent, reuse rather than duplicate;
   - `is_republished` over the fan-out GET;
   - `republish` over the gated read at `current_name`, the read-body child-name rewrite, then `net::author` + `net::record_publish`, signing under `kdf::ipns_keypair(write_seed(freshWriteScopeSeed, node_id))`;
   - `publish_repoint` across the three channels — scope pointer, mailbox, old-root tombstone.
3. **Thread the read-plane material the rewrite needs** — the node's read key, and a nonce from the entropy seam. The read epoch must **not** move: a same-epoch rewrite is not a read rotation and must raise no read-epoch floor (#38 D1, each plane's clock authored by its own authority).
4. **Root linger stays**: `retire` must never include the old root name, and `root_retire_ready` is still stubbed `false` pending the migration-window constant.

## Definition of done

- [x] `blueprint/engine.md` `### rotateScopeWrite` and `blueprint/core.md`'s child-ref carve-out — **done in #1066**, so the blueprint is already normative for this work; read it, don't re-derive it
- [ ] `rotate_write.rs`'s module header narrowed: "The read plane is untouched" is true of keys, seeds and `minReadEpoch`, not of read-body bytes
- [ ] `RepublishedNode`'s doc comment stops promising a byte-stable republish with the read body carried verbatim
- [ ] ADR 0004 `Status:` flipped to `Accepted — implemented in FSM1/cipher-box#<this PR> (merged)` via a follow-up commit on cipher-box-next, per the ADR 0002 precedent

The blueprint is maintained **here**, not in cipher-box-next — that repo's `blueprint/` copies are the as-charted archive and must not be edited.

## Gate

- Resumed name waves via the write-plane history link, and crash recovery from published records only, per #635.
- Register-first ordering enforced **structurally**, so a publish of an unregistered name is impossible rather than merely unlikely.
- After a wave, a read-only holder starting from the re-pointed `currentRootName` resolves **every** node in the subtree — asserted at depth greater than one, so a root-only pass cannot satisfy it.
- Every republished parent's `ChildRef.ipnsName` set equals the derived new names of its children, and no retired name survives anywhere in the subtree's read bodies.
- The read epoch and every read-epoch floor are unchanged across the wave while the write epoch advances — the two planes' clocks stay independently authored.
- A resumed wave that skips already-republished nodes still leaves no stale child name behind.

## Not plumbing — three undecided bindings block the concrete publisher

Attempted on `e935078a1` alongside #1029. #1029 landed clean; this one did not, and the reason is not effort. Three name bindings in already-landed code make the root republish, and the wave's read bodies, unauthorable without a decided answer. Each of them, decided wrongly, mints records this build's own adoption gate rejects — the rule-8 failure mode.

### 1. The scope root's commitment is bound to the record's name

`crates/engine/src/gate/adoption.rs:501` rejects a scope root whose `commitment.ipnsName` is not the name it resolved at, and `crates/engine/src/net/author.rs:176` mirrors that release-active on the encode side. A write rotation moves the root name by construction, so **the root's record cannot be republished byte-stable** — its commitment must be re-signed at the new name first.

`blueprint/engine.md:420` agrees: rotateScopeWrite is "**commitment re-sign**, fresh write override seed, …". But `RotateScopeWritePlan` carries the *current* `commitment`/`commitment_sig` for the owner-only gate and nothing the re-sign needs, and the write-plane committed-set cut is #1019's scope, not this issue's. The two cannot simply be sequenced either: the new root name only exists after `rotate_scope_write` mints the fresh write scope seed, so #1019's cut and this rotation need a decided seam between them.

Note this also falsifies #1019's "Already landed — do not re-implement" claim that the commitment re-sign "is written and simulation-tested" — `rotate_scope_write` never re-signs.

### 2. Blinded tags are bound to the root name

`kdf::blinded_tag(shared, scope_root_ipns_name)` — a grantee's tag binds the scope root's `ipnsName` (`grants/ledger.rs:50`, `:120`). Moving the root name therefore either

- re-mints every ledger row and commitment entry at the new name (a committed-set change — #1019), so surviving grantees re-derive their tag off the re-point object's `currentRootName`; or
- keeps the tags, in which case every grantee's `self_locate` misses and `grants/revocation` reads "no blob at a fresh owner-signed record" as **the definitive revocation signal** — a write rotation would silently read as a mass read-revoke.

This is a security-relevant committed-set decision, not plumbing.

### 3. Every folder's read body pins its children's write-plane names

`ChildRef.ipns_name` (`crates/core/src/seal/body.rs:78`) is the child's write-plane name, and it is what readers navigate by (`sync/project.rs:79` projects it as the node's name). A fresh write scope seed moves every node, so **the wave must rewrite every folder body** with its children's newly derived names — the read plane is untouched in key and epoch, but not in bytes.

`RepublishedNode`'s own doc claims "read-body carried verbatim", which is wrong for any folder whose children moved. And the rewrite is not mechanical: a `ChildRef` pointing at a **descendant scope root** belongs to another write scope, so its name must be left alone; distinguishing the two needs the node's `direct_child_scope_index`, which `WriteScopeNode` does not carry. Getting this wrong strands every read-only grantee on retired names.

### What that means for the shape

Item 1 of this issue (widen `RepublishedNode` vs hand over a resolved-node handle) cannot be answered before 1-3 are: the material the record needs is exactly what those bindings dictate — a re-signed commitment and a re-sealed section for the root, and a *rewritten* body plus the scope index for every folder, not the read body and read key the issue body predicts.

Suggested split, for a human to confirm:

- decide 2 (tag re-mint on a root-name move) — it is the only genuinely open security question, and it is #1019's committed-set surface;
- give #1019 and this issue an explicit seam for the fresh-seed → new-root-name → re-signed-commitment ordering;
- then this issue's remaining surface (`register`/`retire`/`is_republished`/`publish_repoint` over the real seams, plus the structural register-first token) is real plumbing and lands in an afternoon. `net::publish::publish` takes a raw `head_cid`, so the pointer and tombstone channels need no new `PreflightedHead` constructor.

### What did land

#1029 shipped in the same PR, including a defect the composition surfaced: adoption advances the durable sequence floor, so the cascade's resolve and the publish of the same scope root were two reads of one record and the second rejected as not-newer. `OwnerRotationNet` now parks what it gated and the publish takes it.

Two things while the audit finishes.

I fast-forwarded local `main`. It was 5 commits behind `origin/main` — PRs #1120, #1123, #1122, #1119, #1117 were not in the working tree. Now at `2819cb831`.

**I recovered #1026's lost comment.** The only comment on the issue is a literal scratchpad path that was never expanded:

```
@/private/tmp/claude-501/.../scratchpad/1026-comment.md
```

The file still exists on disk. It is a 41-line analysis titled "Not plumbing — three undecided bindings block the concrete publisher", posted 2026-08-04. It names three name bindings that blocked the concrete publisher:

1. The scope root's commitment is bound to the record's name, so a write rotation that moves the root name cannot republish byte-stable — the commitment must be re-signed at the new name first. It also asserts that #1019's "already landed — do not re-implement" claim about the commitment re-sign is false, because `rotate_scope_write` never re-signs.
2. `kdf::blinded_tag(shared, scope_root_ipns_name)` binds a grantee's tag to the root name. Moving the root either re-mints every ledger row, or leaves every grantee's `self_locate` missing — and `grants/revocation` reads a miss as the definitive revocation signal. A write rotation would then read as a mass read-revoke.
3. Every folder's read body pins its children's write-plane names, and a `ChildRef` pointing at a descendant scope root belongs to another write scope and must be left alone.

**Do not repost that comment as-is.** It predates both ADR 0004 and PR #1101, and ADR 0004 explicitly settled binding 3 by deciding the wave rewrites each `ChildRef.ipnsName`. Binding 1 is what #1129 now carves out. Binding 2 — the tag re-mint on a root-name move — is the one the comment calls "the only genuinely open security question", and I have not yet confirmed whether #1101 settled it or whether it is still live.

That is the question the audit is answering: which of these survive on current `main`, which are covered by #1129 and #1130, and which need a new sub-issue. It also verifies all six of #1026's Gate criteria and names the enforcing test for each.

Separately, the wave-7 batch analysis returned and is ready. I will hold it until #1026 is settled, since #1026, #1129, and #1130 sit in the same proposed batch and together are what clears #1019 → #772.

## Scope

`RotationTrigger` at `crates/engine/src/rotation/trigger.rs` enumerates only three of the blueprint's five triggers — `ScopeExit`, `ReadRevoke`, `Manual`. This adds the fourth: **write revoke / downgrade**.

- extend `RotationTrigger` with the write-revoke/downgrade variant and its host-facing `name()` string, and extend the module's trigger table doc to match the blueprint's
- the owner-only committed-set cut for the write plane, mirroring what `revoke_read_grant` does for the read plane: remove or demote the recipient in the grant ledger and the grant-set commitment, owner-re-sign, then drive `rotate_scope_write`

- the revoked writer is absent from the re-signed commitment and the ledger
- surviving write-grantees derive every new name locally — zero re-discovery

The concrete rotation resolvers and publishers over the real seams — this trigger drives `rotate_scope_write`, which needs a production `WriteWavePublisher`.

- #772 — its stated precondition is write-upgrade grants landing, so the mailbox idempotency key can fold in `permission`

Settle one open security question in the CipherBox v2 engine, on current `main`. Local checkout: /Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box, branch `main`, clean, at commit `2819cb831`. Read `AGENTS.md`, `CONTEXT.md`, and `blueprint/engine.md` for the domain language.

- Run the gh CLI as `env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh ...`. Without `env -u`, auth fails.

- Assert behavior from code and tests, never from a source-text grep. A grep hit proves a string exists, not that a path runs.

## The question

A design note written 2026-08-04 (before PR #1101 merged and before ADR 0004) raised three bindings that blocked the concrete write-wave publisher. Two are now settled. The third was called "the only genuinely open security question" and has never been confirmed either way:

> **Blinded tags are bound to the root name.** `kdf::blinded_tag(shared, scope_root_ipns_name)` — a grantee's tag binds the scope root's `ipnsName` (`crates/engine/src/grants/ledger.rs:50`, `:120`). Moving the root name therefore either
> - re-mints every ledger row and commitment entry at the new name (a committed-set change), so surviving grantees re-derive their tag off the re-point object's `currentRootName`; or
> - keeps the tags, in which case every grantee's `self_locate` misses, and `grants/revocation` reads "no blob at a fresh owner-signed record" as **the definitive revocation signal** — so a write rotation would silently read as a mass read-revoke.

A write rotation (`rotate_scope_write`) moves the scope root's IPNS name by construction. So the question is: **after a write-plane name wave, can a surviving read-only grantee still locate its own grant blob, or does the moved root name make its `self_locate` miss and read as a revocation?**

## What to determine

1. **Confirm the binding.** Read `crates/engine/src/grants/ledger.rs` around the `blinded_tag` derivation. Establish exactly which inputs the tag binds — in particular whether the scope root `IpnsName` is one of them, and whether that name is the *write-plane* name that a write rotation moves, or some other stable identifier. This is the crux: if the tag binds a stable scope identifier rather than the moving write-plane name, the whole concern dissolves. Check `CONTEXT.md` for whether "scope root ipns name" is one name or two across the read and write planes.

2. **Trace what a write wave actually does to the grant ledger and the grant-set commitment.** Read `crates/engine/src/rotation/rotate_write.rs` and `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs` (the `WriteWaveNet` impl, `reseal_root`, `publish_moved`, `rewrite_child_names`, `publish_scope_pointer`). Does anything re-mint ledger rows or commitment entries at the new root name? Does the root re-seal carry the ledger through unchanged?

3. **Trace the read side.** Read `self_locate` and the revocation-inference path (`crates/engine/src/grants/` — look at `revocation`, `accept.rs`, `ledger.rs`). Establish precisely what a grantee does when it finds no blob at its tag on a fresh owner-signed record, and whether anything distinguishes "revoked" from "the root moved and my tag is stale".

4. **Decide whether PR #1101 settled it.** Read `env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh pr diff 1101 --repo FSM1/cipher-box`. Also read ADR 0004 (`env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh api /repos/FSM1/cipher-box-next/contents/decisions/0004-read-body-child-names-on-the-name-wave.md --jq '.content' | base64 -d`) and check whether it addresses the tag binding at all.

5. **Decide whether #1019 settles it by scope.** Read issue #1019. Its Scope says it delivers "the owner-only committed-set cut for the write plane, mirroring what `revoke_read_grant` does for the read plane: remove or demote the recipient in the grant ledger and the grant-set commitment, owner-re-sign, then drive `rotate_scope_write`." Its Gate says "a downgrade rotates the write plane only; **the recipient's read grant is still live and their blob still present at their tag afterwards**". Determine whether that Gate criterion, if built as written, would necessarily force the tag re-mint — that is, whether #1019 already owns this work implicitly, or whether #1019 could be built to pass its own gate while the defect survives.

6. **Prove it with a test if you can.** The strongest possible answer is an executed test. Read the existing rotation tests in `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs` (the `#[cfg(test)]` region, around lines 3100-3900) and `crates/engine/tests/write_plane.rs`. If a test already covers a read-only grantee locating its blob *after* a write wave, name it and report its result. If none does, write one in your scratchpad directory ONLY as a patch you do not apply — or, if you can do it without modifying tracked files, describe precisely the test that would settle it and what you predict it returns. Do not commit anything.

## Report back — this is the only thing I see

Answer in this order:

1. **Verdict, one line:** SETTLED (and by what), or LIVE DEFECT, or DISSOLVED (the binding was never what the note claimed).
2. The evidence chain, file:line by file:line, that supports the verdict.

6. Anything adjacent you found that looks wrong and that I did not ask about.

input.content:
## Problem

`WriteWaveNet::publish_scope_pointer` (`crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:1349`) publishes the scope pointer through `publish_inline` and then advances the sequence floor. It never enrols the pointer name in the held set, so neither `keyless_re_put` nor `eol_renew_pass` (`crates/engine/src/net/liveness.rs:105`, `:225`) ever sees it.

The pointer therefore dies at its 90-day client-signed EOL. The API republisher is keyless by design and cannot extend a client-signed validity, so nothing renews it.

## Why it matters

The scope pointer is the **canonical** re-point channel. `publish_repoint` (`net/rotation.rs:1487`) returns `NotLanded` for both `RepointChannel::Mailbox` and `RepointChannel::Tombstone`, so the pointer is currently the only landed channel a read-only survivor has.

A read-only grantee cannot derive the new root name — `open_grant_blob` returns `write_scope_seed: None` for a read-only grant. It learns the new root only by consulting the pointer. Once the pointer's EOL lapses, a cold-starting survivor cannot find the new root at all, and the loss is silent: an unresolvable name is indistinguishable from a name that never existed.

## Complication

`HeldRecord.head_cid` (`liveness.rs:63`) is a required `/ipfs/` head, and a held record with an empty head CID is skipped at `liveness.rs:245`. The pointer's `Value` is the sealed block inline, not a head CID. So the held-set shape cannot carry an inline record as it stands.

## Proposed fix

Give `HeldRecord` an inline-or-head value shape, and enrol the scope pointer at publish time. Keep the release-active empty-head guard for the head variant.

Related: #1043 is the same defect for the vault settings record.

input.content:
## Problem

`WriteWaveNet::publish_repoint` (`crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:1487`) lands one of the three re-point channels the blueprint specifies. `RepointChannel::ScopePointer` publishes. `RepointChannel::Mailbox` and `RepointChannel::Tombstone` return `WritePublishError::NotLanded` unconditionally.

Neither accelerator has a wire shape. No tombstone record type, author, or decoder exists in `crates/engine`. `mailbox::post_sealed` seals internally, so a pre-sealed re-point block would double-seal into a format nothing opens.

The existing test `the_accelerator_channels_report_that_they_did_not_land` (`net/rotation.rs:3478`) pins the shortfall. It does not close it.

## Why it matters

`blueprint/engine.md` "rotateScopeWrite" specifies all three channels. The accelerators are what let a surviving grantee learn of a re-point **before** its next pointer consult. Without them, every survivor's discovery latency is bounded only by the pointer-consult interval, which is exactly the residual #1019's gate says read-only survivors must live within.

The wave completes correctly without them, so this is a discovery-latency defect rather than a trust defect. It must be honest before a production caller ships.

## Proposed fix

Land a tombstone record shape and a mailbox re-point payload, or amend `blueprint/engine.md` to two channels and delete the third variant. Do not leave a specified channel returning `NotLanded`.

Neither accelerator has a wire shape. No tombstone record type, author, or decoder exists in `crates/engine`. `mailbox::post_sealed` seals internally, so a pre-sealed re-point block would double-seal into a format nothing opens.

The existing test `the_accelerator_channels_report_that_they_did_not_land` (`net/rotation.rs:3478`) pins the shortfall. It does not close it.

## Why it matters

`blueprint/engine.md` "rotateScopeWrite" specifies all three channels. The accelerators are what let a surviving grantee learn of a re-point **before** its next pointer consult. Without them, every survivor's discovery latency is bounded only by the pointer-consult interval, which is exactly the residual #1019's gate says read-only survivors must live within.

The wave completes correctly without them, so this is a discovery-latency defect rather than a trust defect. It must be honest before a production caller ships.

## Proposed fix

Land a tombstone record shape and a mailbox re-point payload, or amend `blueprint/engine.md` to two channels and delete the third variant. Do not leave a specified channel returning `NotLanded`.

Decide the migration-window length and its closure signal, then make `root_retire_ready` a real predicate over the re-point publish time rather than a constant. Keep the release-active refusal in `retire` so the root can never be retired early.

## Problem

Nothing in the repo ever mints a `WriteBody.write_history_link`. `reseal_scope_root` copies whatever it is handed (`crates/engine/src/rotation/reseal.rs:467`), and every call site passes `&[]` or passes the old value through — including `WriteWaveNet::reseal_root` (`crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:1232`).

A resumed wave instead takes the fresh write scope seed from `RotateScopeWritePlan::resume_write_scope_seed` (`crates/engine/src/rotation/rotate_write.rs:246`), whose own doc says the recovery wiring is not landed and is faked in tests. The module header repeats this at `rotate_write.rs:38`.

## Why it matters

The crash-recovery tests are real — `mid_wave_crash_resumes_from_published_records_only` (`rotate_write.rs:1243`) and `a_resumed_wave_re_resolves_the_subtree_from_published_records_alone` (`net/rotation.rs:3864`) both pass. They pass because the test hands the seed back in memory.

A real crash has no published source for the seed. The seed is only reachable from the new root, and the new root's name is derived from the seed itself. So after a genuine mid-wave crash the wave cannot resume, and the subtree is stranded half-moved.

#635's own gate names "resumed name waves via the write-plane history link". This is an unmet slice gate, not a nicety.

## Proposed fix

Mint the write-plane history link at the root re-seal so a resumed wave recovers the fresh write scope seed from published state alone. Keep the seam boundary at entropy-versus-published-record, never an in-memory carry.

Related: #764 names the write-plane history link as the mechanism that makes orphaned interior names recoverable, so it depends on this.

## Problem

#1026's gate says "the read epoch and every read-epoch floor are unchanged across the wave while the write epoch advances — the two planes' clocks stay independently authored". No test enforces the floor half of that.

`the_read_epoch_floor_never_moves_across_a_republish` (`crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:3399`) republishes one interior node and checks one floor. The whole-wave test `the_production_edges_carry_the_whole_wave_from_enumeration_to_re_point` (`:3787`) reads no floor at all.

Three floor-touching paths are therefore unasserted:

- the root path, which adopts through `RootAdopter`;
- every proven descendant scope root the enumeration adopts in `record_scope_boundary` (`:1103`);
- the whole-wave composition, where a single mis-ordered adopt could raise a floor that the single-node test would never see.

## Why it matters

A write rotation that raises a read-epoch floor is a cross-plane clock violation (#38 D1 — each plane's clock is authored by its own authority). It would lock out read-plane holders at the old read epoch, and a floor only ever moves forward, so the damage is not recoverable without owner action.

The invariant is currently held by construction and by review, not by a gate.

## Proposed fix

Extend the whole-wave test to snapshot the scope's read-epoch floor and each descendant scope's floor before and after the wave, assert both unchanged, and assert the write-epoch advance in the same test.

## 2. ADR 0004 — full text

Answering your question up front: **ADR 0004 does not mention blinded tags, the grant section, or the grant-set commitment anywhere.** Zero occurrences of "blind", "tag", "grant section", "commitment". It mentions grants only in the phrase "the grant blob carries the write scope seed only for write grants" — used solely to argue that a read-only holder has no `writeScopeSeed`. Its entire subject is `ChildRef.ipnsName` rewriting in read bodies. The root's own name change is treated as already-settled elsewhere (#38 D3, the scope pointer), and the ADR never traces what re-naming the root does to anything keyed by the root's name.

```markdown
# ADR 0004 — Read-body child names are rewritten by the write-plane name wave

- **Status:** Proposed
- **Date:** 2026-08-05
- **Amends:** [#26](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/26) decision D3
  ("Write plane: parallel flat write-seed tree; write rotation = override + child-first
  name wave") — makes concrete what "read-only survivors follow republished mirrors"
  requires, a clause the v2 blueprint dropped
- **Relates to:** [#38](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/38) decision D3
  (the re-point object supplies `currentRootName` only) and
  [#27](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/27) (the child-ref wire format)
- **Implemented by:** [FSM1/cipher-box#1026](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/1026)

## Context

`rotateScopeWrite` mints a fresh write override seed and republishes the scope's whole
subtree under freshly derived names. Every per-node write artefact — `writeSeed`,
`writeKey`, and the Ed25519 IPNS keypair that *is* the `ipnsName` — derives from
`KDF(writeScopeSeed, node.id)`, so a fresh scope seed moves every node in the subtree to
a new name.

D3 of #26 states how each class of party keeps up: "surviving write-grantees derive every
new name locally (zero re-discovery), read-only survivors follow **republished mirrors**
plus the mailbox re-point for the root". #38 D3 later replaced the mailbox with the
owner-signed scope pointer as canonical for the root. The "republished mirrors" half was
never elaborated, and in the v2 blueprint's `### rotateScopeWrite` section it is gone
entirely — the text now reads "read-only survivors follow the owner-signed re-point
object", which covers the root and nothing below it.

That leaves a real hole. A read-only grantee **cannot derive interior names**: the grant
blob carries the write scope seed only for write grants, so a read-only holder has no
`writeScopeSeed` and no way to compute `KDF(writeScopeSeed, node.id)`. The re-point object
carries `currentRootName` and no other name. The only remaining route from the root to a
child is the parent's read-body child list — and `ChildRef` carries an `ipnsName` per
child (#27's wire format). After a name wave those entries name nodes that have moved;
once interior old names batch-retire, they name nothing.

So the wave as specified strands every read-only survivor one level below the root. This
is not an under-implementation of a charted mechanism: no mechanism was ever charted.
The engine's own module text asserts the opposite invariant — "The read plane is
untouched" — which is true of override seeds, read keys and `minReadEpoch`, but not of
read-body *bytes*.

## Decision

**The name wave rewrites read-body child names.** When the wave republishes a node, it
rewrites each `ChildRef.ipnsName` in that node's read body to the child's freshly derived
name and re-seals the read body under the node's unchanged read key at the unchanged read
epoch. The existing child-first ordering already makes every child's new name known
before its parent publishes, so no second pass is needed.

Three consequences follow and are accepted as part of this decision:

1. **The republish is not byte-stable.** The read body changes, so the record cannot be
   reproduced verbatim from its predecessor. Any "carry the read body verbatim" language
   in the blueprint or in `rotateScopeWrite`'s contract is withdrawn.
2. **The publisher needs read-plane material** — the node's read key, and a nonce from
   the entropy seam for the re-seal. The write rotation therefore touches read-plane
   bytes while leaving read-plane *keys and epochs* untouched; the blueprint must say
   the narrower thing rather than "the read plane is untouched".
3. **The read epoch does not move.** A rewrite at the same epoch is not a read rotation
   and must not raise any read-epoch floor; `minReadEpoch` still carries unchanged, per
   #38 D1's rule that each plane's clock is authored by its own authority.

### Rejected alternatives

**Resolve children by node id through a write-plane index**, removing names from the read
body. Correct in the abstract — location-independent ids are what the write plane already
uses — but it is a `crates/core` wire-format change to #27's `ChildRef`, and it would
leave a read-only grantee needing a name lookup they still cannot perform. Rejected as
out of scope and insufficient on its own.

**Tombstone every migrated interior name** and let readers chase `movedTo`, instead of
rewriting anything. Rejected: #33's chase is depth-guarded, so a subtree deeper than the
guard breaks outright; and old names lapse at the 90-day EOL, so the approach defers the
break rather than removing it. It also multiplies the wave's publish count by keeping a
live tombstone per interior node, against #34 D4's retirement path.

## Consequences

- Read-only survivors traverse the subtree normally after a wave, which is what #26 D3
  intended and what its "republished mirrors" clause was pointing at.
- `rotateScopeWrite` is no longer describable as write-plane-only. The blueprint entry and
  the engine module header both need correcting; the honest statement is that the wave
  rewrites read-plane *metadata* while never re-keying it.
- Content bytes are still never re-encrypted (#26 D6). Only the child-name field of a
  folder's read body changes.
- The wave's cost per node rises by one read-body re-seal. It stays O(subtree) and stays
  background and parallel, so the shape of the cost is unchanged.
- A resumed wave is unaffected: `isRepublished` still answers from published state alone,
  and a node whose record already sits at the new name is skipped before any re-seal.

## Gate

- After a wave, a read-only holder starting from the re-pointed `currentRootName`
  resolves every node in the subtree — asserted at a depth greater than one, so a
  root-only pass cannot satisfy it.
- Every republished parent's `ChildRef.ipnsName` set equals the derived new names of its
  children, and no retired name survives anywhere in the subtree's read bodies.
- The read epoch and every read-epoch floor are unchanged across the wave, while the
  write epoch advances — the two planes' clocks stay independently authored.
- A resumed wave that skips already-republished nodes still leaves no stale child name
  behind.
```

## 2. ADR 0004 — full text

Answering your question up front: **ADR 0004 does not mention blinded tags, the grant section, or the grant-set commitment anywhere.** Zero occurrences of "blind", "tag", "grant section", "commitment". It mentions grants only in the phrase "the grant blob carries the write scope seed only for write grants" — used solely to argue that a read-only holder has no `writeScopeSeed`. Its entire subject is `ChildRef.ipnsName` rewriting in read bodies. The root's own name change is treated as already-settled elsewhere (#38 D3, the scope pointer), and the ADR never traces what re-naming the root does to anything keyed by the root's name.

```markdown
# ADR 0004 — Read-body child names are rewritten by the write-plane name wave

- **Status:** Proposed
- **Date:** 2026-08-05
- **Amends:** [#26](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/26) decision D3
  ("Write plane: parallel flat write-seed tree; write rotation = override + child-first
  name wave") — makes concrete what "read-only survivors follow republished mirrors"
  requires, a clause the v2 blueprint dropped
- **Relates to:** [#38](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/38) decision D3
  (the re-point object supplies `currentRootName` only) and
  [#27](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/issues/27) (the child-ref wire format)
- **Implemented by:** [FSM1/cipher-box#1026](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/1026)

## Context

`rotateScopeWrite` mints a fresh write override seed and republishes the scope's whole
subtree under freshly derived names. Every per-node write artefact — `writeSeed`,
`writeKey`, and the Ed25519 IPNS keypair that *is* the `ipnsName` — derives from
`KDF(writeScopeSeed, node.id)`, so a fresh scope seed moves every node in the subtree to
a new name.

D3 of #26 states how each class of party keeps up: "surviving write-grantees derive every
new name locally (zero re-discovery), read-only survivors follow **republished mirrors**
plus the mailbox re-point for the root". #38 D3 later replaced the mailbox with the
owner-signed scope pointer as canonical for the root. The "republished mirrors" half was
never elaborated, and in the v2 blueprint's `### rotateScopeWrite` section it is gone
entirely — the text now reads "read-only survivors follow the owner-signed re-point
object", which covers the root and nothing below it.

That leaves a real hole. A read-only grantee **cannot derive interior names**: the grant
blob carries the write scope seed only for write grants, so a read-only holder has no
`writeScopeSeed` and no way to compute `KDF(writeScopeSeed, node.id)`. The re-point object
carries `currentRootName` and no other name. The only remaining route from the root to a
child is the parent's read-body child list — and `ChildRef` carries an `ipnsName` per
child (#27's wire format). After a name wave those entries name nodes that have moved;
once interior old names batch-retire, they name nothing.

So the wave as specified strands every read-only survivor one level below the root. This
is not an under-implementation of a charted mechanism: no mechanism was ever charted.
The engine's own module text asserts the opposite invariant — "The read plane is
untouched" — which is true of override seeds, read keys and `minReadEpoch`, but not of
read-body *bytes*.

## Decision

**The name wave rewrites read-body child names.** When the wave republishes a node, it
rewrites each `ChildRef.ipnsName` in that node's read body to the child's freshly derived
name and re-seals the read body under the node's unchanged read key at the unchanged read
epoch. The existing child-first ordering already makes every child's new name known
before its parent publishes, so no second pass is needed.

Three consequences follow and are accepted as part of this decision:

1. **The republish is not byte-stable.** The read body changes, so the record cannot be
   reproduced verbatim from its predecessor. Any "carry the read body verbatim" language
   in the blueprint or in `rotateScopeWrite`'s contract is withdrawn.
2. **The publisher needs read-plane material** — the node's read key, and a nonce from
   the entropy seam for the re-seal. The write rotation therefore touches read-plane
   bytes while leaving read-plane *keys and epochs* untouched; the blueprint must say
   the narrower thing rather than "the read plane is untouched".
3. **The read epoch does not move.** A rewrite at the same epoch is not a read rotation
   and must not raise any read-epoch floor; `minReadEpoch` still carries unchanged, per
   #38 D1's rule that each plane's clock is authored by its own authority.

### Rejected alternatives

**Resolve children by node id through a write-plane index**, removing names from the read
body. Correct in the abstract — location-independent ids are what the write plane already
uses — but it is a `crates/core` wire-format change to #27's `ChildRef`, and it would
leave a read-only grantee needing a name lookup they still cannot perform. Rejected as
out of scope and insufficient on its own.

**Tombstone every migrated interior name** and let readers chase `movedTo`, instead of
rewriting anything. Rejected: #33's chase is depth-guarded, so a subtree deeper than the
guard breaks outright; and old names lapse at the 90-day EOL, so the approach defers the
break rather than removing it. It also multiplies the wave's publish count by keeping a
live tombstone per interior node, against #34 D4's retirement path.

## Consequences

- Read-only survivors traverse the subtree normally after a wave, which is what #26 D3
  intended and what its "republished mirrors" clause was pointing at.
- `rotateScopeWrite` is no longer describable as write-plane-only. The blueprint entry and
  the engine module header both need correcting; the honest statement is that the wave
  rewrites read-plane *metadata* while never re-keying it.
- Content bytes are still never re-encrypted (#26 D6). Only the child-name field of a
  folder's read body changes.
- The wave's cost per node rises by one read-body re-seal. It stays O(subtree) and stays
  background and parallel, so the shape of the cost is unchanged.
- A resumed wave is unaffected: `isRepublished` still answers from published state alone,
  and a node whose record already sits at the new name is skipped before any re-seal.

## Gate

- After a wave, a read-only holder starting from the re-pointed `currentRootName`
  resolves every node in the subtree — asserted at a depth greater than one, so a
  root-only pass cannot satisfy it.
- Every republished parent's `ChildRef.ipnsName` set equals the derived new names of its
  children, and no retired name survives anywhere in the subtree's read bodies.
- The read epoch and every read-epoch floor are unchanged across the wave, while the
  write epoch advances — the two planes' clocks stay independently authored.
- A resumed wave that skips already-republished nodes still leaves no stale child name
  behind.
```

## 3. The failure sequence and blast radius

1. Owner shares folder F read-only with Alice. `create_read_grant` (`create.rs:302,307`) files Alice's blob under `T_old = blinded_tag(ECDH(owner,alice), N_old)`.
2. Owner later downgrades Bob from write to read, or does a manual write-hygiene rotate. Either drives `rotate_scope_write`.
3. The wave mints a fresh `writeScopeSeed`; the root moves `N_old → N_new` (`rotate_write.rs:529`).
4. `reseal_root` publishes at `N_new` with `commitment.ipns_name = N_new`, owner-signed, and Alice's blob still filed under `T_old` (`net/rotation.rs:1203`, `reseal.rs:356`).
5. Alice follows the canonical scope-pointer re-point to `currentRootName = N_new`, resolves, passes the adoption gate, derives `T_new = blinded_tag(ECDH, N_new)`, and finds nothing.
6. `classify` returns `RevocationSignal` — the *definitive* "you were removed", outranking epoch lag by design (`revocation.rs:78-80`).

**Blast radius: every read-only grantee of the rotated scope, plus every write grantee that self-locates rather than deriving.** A write revoke aimed at one recipient silently reads as a mass read-revoke of the whole grant set. It is not self-healing: the tag is a pure function of the name, so every subsequent poll returns the same verdict.

**Recoverable only by owner action**, and only awkwardly — the owner must re-mint at the current name and republish. There is no client-side recovery, because after a second rotation the mint-time name is unrecoverable (`RepointObject.prev_root` carries exactly one hop, `rotate_write.rs:431`).

**Not yet exploitable in production.** `rotate_scope_write` has no facade or trigger caller (only tests and `net/rotation.rs` compose it), and `grants::revocation::classify` has no production caller at all — its only uses are the public re-export and `crates/engine/tests/grants_mailbox.rs`. This is a landed defect on an unwired path, so the cost of fixing it now is a ~15-line change in `reseal_root`, not a migration.

## The security question is a live defect

Not settled by #1101, not settled by #1019. Proven by execution against production code, then re-verified by me directly:

`reseal_root` (`net/rotation.rs:1202`) overwrites **only** `commitment.ipns_name` with the new root name and owner-re-signs. It clones `commitment.entries` and passes `grant_ledger` through verbatim. `reseal.rs:356` then files every freshly sealed blob under `entry.tag` off that carried row. So the record owner-asserts the new name while every tag inside it binds the old one. `enforce_committed_ledger` compares tags against tags — both stale the same way — so nothing fails closed.

A read-only survivor follows the re-point, passes the adoption gate (which forces `commitment.ipns_name == candidate.name`), re-derives its tag from that name, and misses. `classify` returns `RevocationSignal` on `!blob_present` **before** any epoch check. One write revoke or downgrade reads as a mass read-revoke of the whole grant set, not self-healing and not recoverable client-side, because `RepointObject.prev_root` carries one hop.

No test catches it because every wave fixture commits an empty grant set. The blind spot is structural: `RepublishedNode` deliberately carries no owner material, so the pure `rotate_scope_write` simulation can never reach this class.

**#1019 cannot pass its own gate.** Its Gate says the downgraded recipient's blob is still present at their tag afterwards. That is unsatisfiable on `main`. But #1019's "Already landed — do not re-implement" section fences `rotate_scope_write` out of scope. An implementer following it literally would either reach outside the issue's scope or write the assertion against the stale tag and ship a green test over broken behaviour.

**#1127 must sequence behind #1135.** #1127's proposed check refuses a row whose `recipientEncPk` does not re-derive its tag. On the write-wave path that fires on every *honest* row and aborts any wave over a scope with grants. Re-mint first, then #1127's check is a tautology at the mint site.

## What this costs the wave-7 plan

**#1016 is no longer actionable.** It was rank 2 on the critical path and the proposed sequence-first batch. Wiring the facade rotation and grant command arms gives `rotate_scope_write` its first production caller, and #1135 is exactly what must not be reachable from production. #1135 is a roughly 15-line change in `reseal_root` plus a non-empty-grant-set fixture, so it is cheap — but it now gates the wave's head.

- **ADR 0004's status flip** stays a checkbox on #1026 rather than an issue, since it is one commit on cipher-box-next. #1026 therefore still cannot close. Say the word and I will make that commit.
- **The content-CID question** — `publish_moved` publishes with `content_cids: Vec::new()`, so after a wave every node's pins remain accounted to its retired name. #1125 covers the register-versus-retire derivation but not the name-move case. engine: bind a re-sealed grant blob to the tag its recipient key derives
## Problem

`reseal_scope_root` seals each grant blob to `entry.recipient_enc_pk` taken straight from the resolved write-body ledger, with no re-derivation of the tag it is filed under (`crates/engine/src/rotation/reseal.rs`, the grant-blob loop).

`enforce_committed_ledger` compares `(tag, permission)` only — its own doc states that `recipientIdentityPk`, `recipientEncPk` and `expiresAt` "go unchecked here and a write-grantee may alter them undetectably". So a write-grantee that swaps a victim's `recipientEncPk` makes every subsequent honest re-seal — the owner's included — wrap the scope seed to the attacker's key under the victim's owner-committed tag. Owner authority passes at every step, and the victim simply stops being able to open its blob.

## Fix

The owner (and any re-sealer holding the owner encryption subkey) can re-derive the tag cheaply and refuse a row whose `recipientEncPk` does not produce the tag it is filed under. `crates/engine/src/grants/invite.rs`'s `convert_invite_claim` already does exactly this check against a recorded link:

```rust
let link_enc = X25519Public::from_bytes(link.ephemeral_enc_pk).ok_or(...)?;
if recipient_blinded_tag(owner.enc_secret, &link_enc, name) != Some(link.tag) { ... }
```

A re-sealer that is a write-grantee rather than the owner holds no owner encryption subkey and cannot run it, so the check has to be conditional on the material available — which is also the honest statement of the residual that remains.

## Gate

Rotation simulation: a re-seal over a ledger whose `recipientEncPk` was swapped under a committed tag must fail closed rather than wrap the seed to the swapped key, when the re-sealer holds the owner encryption subkey.

## Origin

Found by the `/crypto-privacy-review` gate on the grant-invite claim PR. Out of that PR's file ownership (`crates/engine/src/rotation/` belonged to a sibling slice), and strictly more severe than the in-diff residual it was found next to.

Design is clear, and the two fixes compose so that one proves the other:

- **#1135** — `reseal_root` re-mints each ledger row at the new root name before it re-seals, using `mint_grant_row(owner_enc_secret, identity_pk, enc_pk, scope_id, new_name, permission)`, which returns the tag, the commitment entry, and the ledger row together so they cannot drift apart.
- **#1127** — `reseal_scope_root` takes an optional owner encryption subkey and, when it has one, refuses any row whose `recipient_enc_pk` does not re-derive the tag it is filed under **at `identity.ipns_name`**.

On the read-rotation path the name does not move, so the check validates the carried rows. On the write-wave path `identity.ipns_name` is the *new* name, so the check fires unless the re-mint already happened. #1127 becomes the gate that enforces #1135 rather than a separate guard.

Note especially the code-style rules on comments (short, explain *why*, no absence-justifying comments, no apologia, no bare tracker references) and **security rule 8** (encode/decode fail-closed symmetry — release-active `Err`, never `debug_assert!`).

## The two issues

- **#1135** `engine: the write name wave republishes grant tags bound to the retired root name`
- **#1127** `engine: bind a re-sealed grant blob to the tag its recipient key derives`

Read both bodies via REST (`gh issue view` is broken repo-wide — Projects-classic GraphQL deprecation):
`env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh api /repos/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/1135 --jq '.body'` and the same for 1127.
Always run gh as `env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh ...` or auth fails.

## The defect, in one paragraph

`kdf::blinded_tag(ecdh_shared, scope_root_ipns_name)` (`crates/core/src/kdf/mod.rs:285`) binds the scope root's `ipnsName`. A write rotation mints a fresh `writeScopeSeed` and moves the root name by construction (`crates/engine/src/rotation/rotate_write.rs:486-529`). `WriteWaveNet::reseal_root` (`crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:1195-1238`) rewrites `commitment.ipns_name` to the new name and owner-re-signs it, but clones `commitment.entries` and passes `plane.write_body.grant_ledger` through verbatim. `reseal_scope_root` (`crates/engine/src/rotation/reseal.rs`, the grant-blob loop around `:330-360`) then files each freshly sealed blob under `entry.tag` off that carried row. So the published record owner-asserts the new name while every tag inside it binds the retired one. A surviving grantee re-derives its tag from the name the record asserts, misses, and `classify` (`crates/engine/src/grants/revocation.rs:74`) reads that as the definitive revocation signal. One write revoke reads as a mass read-revoke.

Separately (#1127), `reseal_scope_root` trusts `entry.recipient_enc_pk` verbatim, so a write-grantee that swaps a victim's `recipientEncPk` under the victim's owner-committed tag redirects every future honest re-seal, the owner's included.

## The agreed design — implement exactly this

The two fixes compose so that the second enforces the first.

1. **#1135 — re-mint in `reseal_root`.** Before calling `reseal_scope_root`, `WriteWaveNet::reseal_root` re-mints every grant row at `node.new_name` using `mint_grant_row` (`crates/engine/src/grants/ledger.rs:113`), which returns `{tag, commitment_entry, ledger_entry}` together so the three cannot drift apart. It already holds everything needed: `self.owner_enc_secret` (`net/rotation.rs:1207`), `self.scope_id`, `node.new_name`, and each carried row's `recipient_identity_pk` and `recipient_enc_pk`. Build the new `commitment.entries` and the new `grant_ledger` from the re-minted rows, then owner-re-sign the commitment over both the new `ipns_name` and the new entries.

2. **#1127 — verify in `reseal_scope_root`.** Give `reseal_scope_root` an optional owner encryption subkey (an `Option<&X25519Secret>`; put it on `ScopeRootIdentity` or `CommittedSet`, whichever reads better — justify your choice in the PR body, not in a code comment). When it is `Some`, every ledger row must satisfy `recipient_blinded_tag(owner_enc_secret, recipient_enc_pub, identity.ipns_name) == Some(entry.tag)`, else fail closed with a new `ResealError` variant **before any seal**. When it is `None` (a write-grantee re-sealer, which holds no owner encryption subkey), skip the check — that residual is honest and must be stated in the doc comment.

Why this composes: on the read-rotation path the name does not move, so the check validates the carried rows. On the write-wave path `identity.ipns_name` is the new name, so the check fires unless the re-mint already happened.

## Details you must get right

- **`expires_at` must survive the re-mint.** `GrantLedgerEntry::new` does not take it — check the type and preserve each row's existing `expires_at` onto the re-minted row. Losing it would silently un-expire every grant. Verify this with a test.
- **`mint_grant_row` returns `Option`** — `None` on a non-contributory ECDH. Refuse fail-closed; do not unwrap.
- **`recipient_identity_pk` is stored sec1-encoded** on `GrantLedgerEntry`. You need an `EcdsaVerifier` for `mint_grant_row`. A row whose stored identity key does not parse must fail closed.
- **Fix the false doc comment.** `reseal.rs` around `:304-307` currently says "the tag<->enc_pk binding is enforced at resolve time", and `grants/ledger.rs:170-175`'s `enforce_committed_ledger` doc makes the same claim. **No such resolve-time check exists.** Both comments must become true statements about what the code now does. Keep them short.
- **Update every call site** of `reseal_scope_root`. Find them with ripgrep across `crates/`. The cascade/read-rotation callers should pass the owner secret when they hold it.
- Preserve the existing fail-closed ordering: every new check happens **before** anything is sealed.
- Do not weaken or reorder the existing `SignerNotCommitted`, `TooManyHistoryLinks`, `TooManyCommittedGrants`, or `enforce_committed_ledger` checks.

## Tests — this is the point of the PR

The reason this defect survived is that **every existing wave fixture commits an empty grant set** (`crates/engine/src/testkit/owner_root.rs:191`, `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:2371`, `:2401`). Fix that.

1. A rotation simulation over a scope root with a **non-empty** grant set: a read-only grantee re-deriving `recipient_blinded_tag(…, outcome.new_root_name)` locates its blob in the republished section.

3. `expires_at` survives the re-mint.
4. #1127's gate: a re-seal over a ledger whose `recipient_enc_pk` was swapped under a committed tag fails closed rather than wrapping the seed to the swapped key, when the re-sealer holds the owner encryption subkey.
5. The `None` path still re-seals successfully (the write-grantee re-sealer residual).
6. A release-build-active test for the new fail-closed check (security rule 8) — it must not rely on `debug_assert!`.

Write the tests first, watch them fail, then implement. Assert behavior, never source text.

Piping a gate through `tail` has previously given a false 0 and pushed a break to CI.

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — **`--all`, never scoped to `-p`**, that is the CI gate exactly

- `cargo test --workspace`

If you touched anything under `crates/core`, also run the core KAT suite.

Always run gh as `env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh ...` or auth fails.

## The defect, in one paragraph

`kdf::blinded_tag(ecdh_shared, scope_root_ipns_name)` (`crates/core/src/kdf/mod.rs:285`) binds the scope root's `ipnsName`. So the published record owner-asserts the new name while every tag inside it binds the retired one. A surviving grantee re-derives its tag from the name the record asserts, misses, and `classify` (`crates/engine/src/grants/revocation.rs:74`) reads that as the definitive revocation signal. One write revoke reads as a mass read-revoke.

Separately (#1127), `reseal_scope_root` trusts `entry.recipient_enc_pk` verbatim, so a write-grantee that swaps a victim's `recipientEncPk` under the victim's owner-committed tag redirects every future honest re-seal, the owner's included.

The two fixes compose so that the second enforces the first.

1. **#1135 — re-mint in `reseal_root`.** Before calling `reseal_scope_root`, `WriteWaveNet::reseal_root` re-mints every grant row at `node.new_name` using `mint_grant_row` (`crates/engine/src/grants/ledger.rs:113`), which returns `{tag, commitment_entry, ledger_entry}` together so the three cannot drift apart. It already holds everything needed: `self.owner_enc_secret` (`net/rotation.rs:1207`), `self.scope_id`, `node.new_name`, and each carried row's `recipient_identity_pk` and `recipient_enc_pk`. Build the new `commitment.entries` and the new `grant_ledger` from the re-minted rows, then owner-re-sign the commitment over both the new `ipns_name` and the new entries.

2. **#1127 — verify in `reseal_scope_root`.** Give `reseal_scope_root` an optional owner encryption subkey (an `Option<&X25519Secret>`; put it on `ScopeRootIdentity` or `CommittedSet`, whichever reads better — justify your choice in the PR body, not in a code comment). When it is `Some`, every ledger row must satisfy `recipient_blinded_tag(owner_enc_secret, recipient_enc_pub, identity.ipns_name) == Some(entry.tag)`, else fail closed with a new `ResealError` variant **before any seal**. When it is `None` (a write-grantee re-sealer, which holds no owner encryption subkey), skip the check — that residual is honest and must be stated in the doc comment.

Why this composes: on the read-rotation path the name does not move, so the check validates the carried rows. On the write-wave path `identity.ipns_name` is the new name, so the check fires unless the re-mint already happened.

## Details you must get right

- **`expires_at` must survive the re-mint.** `GrantLedgerEntry::new` does not take it — check the type and preserve each row's existing `expires_at` onto the re-minted row. Losing it would silently un-expire every grant. Verify this with a test.
- **`mint_grant_row` returns `Option`** — `None` on a non-contributory ECDH. Refuse fail-closed; do not unwrap.
- **`recipient_identity_pk` is stored sec1-encoded** on `GrantLedgerEntry`. You need an `EcdsaVerifier` for `mint_grant_row`. A row whose stored identity key does not parse must fail closed.
- **Fix the false doc comment.** `reseal.rs` around `:304-307` currently says "the tag<->enc_pk binding is enforced at resolve time", and `grants/ledger.rs:170-175`'s `enforce_committed_ledger` doc makes the same claim. **No such resolve-time check exists.** Both comments must become true statements about what the code now does. Keep them short.
- **Update every call site** of `reseal_scope_root`. Find them with ripgrep across `crates/`. The cascade/read-rotation callers should pass the owner secret when they hold it.
- Preserve the existing fail-closed ordering: every new check happens **before** anything is sealed.
- Do not weaken or reorder the existing `SignerNotCommitted`, `TooManyHistoryLinks`, `TooManyCommittedGrants`, or `enforce_committed_ledger` checks.

## Tests — this is the point of the PR

The reason this defect survived is that **every existing wave fixture commits an empty grant set** (`crates/engine/src/testkit/owner_root.rs:191`, `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs:2371`, `:2401`). Fix that.

Required coverage, and each test must fail on `main` before your change:

1. A rotation simulation over a scope root with a **non-empty** grant set: a read-only grantee re-deriving `recipient_blinded_tag(…, outcome.new_root_name)` locates its blob in the republished section.
2. The same at depth greater than one, and with **both** a read row and a write row in the ledger.
3. `expires_at` survives the re-mint.
4. #1127's gate: a re-seal over a ledger whose `recipient_enc_pk` was swapped under a committed tag fails closed rather than wrapping the seed to the swapped key, when the re-sealer holds the owner encryption subkey.
5. The `None` path still re-seals successfully (the write-grantee re-sealer residual).
6. A release-build-active test for the new fail-closed check (security rule 8) — it must not rely on `debug_assert!`.

Write the tests first, watch them fail, then implement. Assert behavior, never source text.

## Gates — all must pass, run each UNPIPED and read `$?`

Piping a gate through `tail` has previously given a false 0 and pushed a break to CI.

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — **`--all`, never scoped to `-p`**, that is the CI gate exactly
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test --workspace`
- `cargo check -p cipherbox-wasm --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` — `--workspace` never builds wasm32, and a break here is invisible until the Core KATs / Client Browser Suite gate

If you touched anything under `crates/core`, also run the core KAT suite.

- Branch `fix/rotation-grant-tag-remint` off `main`. **Never push to `main`.**
- Conventional Commits. No parenthesized text in the subject line (it breaks Release Please).
- Suggested PR title: `fix(engine): re-mint grant tags on the write name wave and bind a re-sealed blob to its derived tag`
- Commit signing can hang on the 1Password agent — if a commit hangs, guard it with `timeout`, and **never** pass `--no-gpg-sign`.
- **Open the PR as a DRAFT.** Body must say `Closes #1135` and `Closes #1127`. No Claude/AI attribution anywhere in the PR body or commits.
- If `gh pr edit` fails on Projects-classic, use `env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh api -X PATCH /repos/FSM1/cipher-box/pulls/<N> -F body=@file`.
- Note: creating a PR can trigger a bot release commit, so any later push needs a `git fetch` + rebase first.

## Report back — the only thing I see

- The PR number and URL, and confirmation it is a draft.
- The design choice you made for where the owner secret lives, and why.
- Each gate command with its exit code.
- The list of tests you added, and confirmation each one fails on `main`.
- Anything you found that contradicts the brief above — the brief is my reading of the code, not ground truth. If the code disagrees, follow the code and tell me.

Write prose in Simplified Technical English: short active sentences, active voice, no contractions, no idioms.

When batching v2 issues into parallel PRs, the binding constraint is hot-file contention, not the
number of actionable issues. Re-confirmed 2026-08-04 against main `3c08517d3` after six merges.

Standing hot files:

- `crates/engine/src/facade.rs` (5300+) and `crates/engine/tests/write_plane.rs` (4800+) — touched
  by almost every engine issue
- `crates/engine/src/sync/drain.rs` — settings, op-queue, pin-provider, device-state clusters
- `crates/engine/src/gate/floor.rs` + `seams/floor_store.rs`
- `crates/wasm/src/seams_bridge.rs` — NOT `host.rs`; seam-shape changes land next door to host.rs
- `apps/web/src/engine/snapshotStore.ts`, `packages/client/src/leaderRelay.ts`

The #635 rotation cluster is its own contention zone — `rotation/trigger.rs` (279 lines, 3
contenders), `net/rotation.rs`, `rotation/rotate_write.rs`, `rotation/sweep.rs`,
`rotation/reseal.rs` + `rotate.rs`.

**Why:** facade.rs is 5000+ lines so different functions usually auto-merge, but signature/shape
changes ripple. The recurring failure is the semantic merge conflict in
[[project-semantic-merge-conflict-shape-change]] — two PRs both MERGEABLE that break main's compile
pairwise.

**How to apply:** batch so each PR *owns* its hot files exclusively, and sequence any PR carrying a
signature change ahead of everything touching its callers. Group small issues that collide on the
same interface into ONE PR rather than trying to parallelize them — this also conserves the
CodeRabbit quota (see [[feedback-keep-prs-draft-control-cr-timing.md]]). Reserve worktree isolation
for the batches that genuinely run concurrently.

**Re-confirm the map after every merge wave.** Closing issues retires rows, but merges also *create*
rows — and a file's contenders are not always the ones named in the issue bodies (e.g. #793 reads as
a `gate/adoption.rs` issue but also edits `rotation/reseal.rs`, colliding with a different wave).
Repo-wide sweeps like a comment-hygiene pass collide with everything; run them alone.

tag↔enc_pk binding "is a resolve-time check". No such check exists anywhere on the resolve path.

label saying so, so every actionable-set query keeps proposing it.
